title: The Case of the Backwards Cattle
label: A Bizzing mystery
setting: the Homeric Hymn to Hermes: Pieria, Onchestus, Mount Cyllene and Olympus
sourceText: the Homeric Hymn to Hermes (Hymn 4), retold; quoted lines from H. G. Evelyn-White's translation (Loeb, 1914)

card.text:
The painted door has opened at last.
Through it is a hillside in the Greek myths, and a very upset god.
Apollo's fifty cows have vanished in the night.
Every hoof-print points into the meadow. Not one points out.
At sunset, Zeus will judge, and someone will pay.
Read the tracks, {det}.
Tracks are a text too.

cutscene.place: The office, the morning after Case 3
cutscene.picture: The office, the morning after Case 3. The painted Door stands ajar. Ink fills its keyhole like a tiny well. The room smells of wild thyme, which nobody in Inkwell grows. {det}'s persona sign is in the panel: the owl's shadow on the round window / the laces lifting / two crows on the lamp post / a strand of yellow wool on the floorboards / a tab of the notebook turned to gold / one soft note in the air. NELL: "Every key in town. Nothing. And now it just… opens?"

Quill on the desk, small deerstalker on. QUILL: "Three rules. One: inside a story, you can find out anything. You can't change what the story is. Two: bring back what you learned, not what you found. Three: mind the time. A story keeps its own clock." NELL: "And this one?" QUILL: "Closes at sunset. I'll hold the Door."

cutscene.place: Through the Door: Pieria at dawn
cutscene.picture: Through the Door: Pieria at dawn. A wide meadow on a hillside, mist in the hollows, wild thyme in purple cushions, a sea far below. The meadow is empty. Only the grass by the gate is flattened, as if a crowd had stood there.
Apollo, golden and enormous, holding his own head in both hands. He is drawn upset and comic, never frightening. APOLLO: "My cattle! Fifty of them! Counted, every one!"

Apollo, pointing down the long road south. APOLLO: "At sunset my father will judge. Somebody will pay for my cows. That old man down at Onchestus saw something. I know it." NELL: "Hunch-o-meter's already twitching."

cast.name: The old man of Onchestus
cast.look: Bent and brown as a vine root, a straw hat, a pruning knife on a cord, brushwood in his beard
cast.manner: Talks in circles; bad at keeping quiet and knows it
cast.note: Motive: Apollo's cows ate his best vines last spring. · Secret: last night he promised a small stranger to "see nothing", and he is trying very hard to keep a promise he never wanted

cast.name: Maia
cast.look: Dark hair loose, a blue cloak sewn with tiny silver stars, a cave lamp
cast.manner: Gentle, tired, protective; answers a question with a question when cornered
cast.note: Motive: she and her son live in a cold cave with no herds and no honours. · Secret: yesterday she left the baby sleeping and went up the mountain to sit with her six sisters all day, and she is ashamed of it

cast.name: Hermes, one day old
cast.look: A baby in a woven cradle, huge innocent eyes, one curl, swaddled to the chin; something lumpy under the blanket
cast.manner: Butter-wouldn't-melt; far too good with words for one day old
cast.note: Motive: he wants a herd and honour, like his big brother. · Secret: under the blanket is a thing nobody has ever seen: the first lyre

cast.name: Apollo
cast.look: Golden, enormous, a laurel wreath askew, a silver bow on his back that he never touches
cast.manner: Big, comic, frantic; kind underneath; stamps when upset and the hill shakes a little

cast.name: Kleon, Apollo's herald 🪔
cast.look: A thin young man with a herald's staff, wax tablets on a strap, sandals worn to string

cast.name: Zeus
cast.look: Vast, white-bearded, sitting on a cloud like an armchair; a soft rumble of thunder when he chuckles
cast.manner: Grave for one minute, then laughs

docs.title: Tablet
docs.author: Apollo, cut into wax by his herald
docs.where: propped on the gate-post of the empty meadow
docs.picture: a herald's wax tablet in a wooden frame, the wax scratched in neat lines, a sprig of laurel tucked in the hinge.
docs.body:
Hear this!
[[c:fifty|Yesterday afternoon I counted my cattle. Fifty cows, all here.]]
[[c:sunset-left|At sunset I went up to Olympus to sing.]]
[[c:empty|At dawn I came back. The meadow is empty.]]
[[c:noon|Yesterday at noon I heard a new sound from the south.]]
[[c:bowstring|It was like a bowstring that had learned to sing.]]
I thought nothing of it.
[[c:wolf-theory|A wolf has done this, or a thief.]]
At sunset, Zeus will judge.
— Apollo

docs.title: Report
docs.author: Kleon, herald of Apollo
docs.where: read aloud by Kleon at the gate, then pinned to the post
docs.picture: a second wax tablet with a little sketch scratched in the corner: a hoof-print, drawn as two curved half-moons.
docs.body:
THE TRACKS, AS I READ THEM
[[c:tracks-in|Every hoof-print points into the meadow.]]
[[c:none-out|Not one print points out.]]
Fifty cows cannot walk in and melt away.
[[c:trail|A trail of trampled grass runs south, over the hill.]]
[[c:trail-north|On that trail, every print still faces north, towards the meadow.]]
[[c:no-wolf|There are no wolf prints anywhere.]]
— Kleon, herald

docs.title: Report
docs.author: Kleon, herald of Apollo
docs.where: on the trail, two hills south
docs.picture: a tablet with a careful sketch of one odd print: a big, ragged oval with a small round dent in the middle.
docs.body:
THE ODD PRINTS
Beside the cow tracks run other prints.
[[c:broom|They are large and brushy at the edges, like a broom that walked.]]
[[c:not-man|They are not a man's. They are not a woman's. They are not a wolf's.]]
[[c:fig|In the middle of each is a dent no bigger than a fig.]]
[[c:zigzag|They wander from side to side across the trail.]]
The trail runs on, towards the vineyards of Onchestus.
— Kleon

docs.title: List
docs.author: Kleon, herald of Apollo
docs.where: where the trail meets a river, far to the south, below a mountain
docs.picture: a tablet listing three finds, with the finds themselves laid on a flat stone beside it: a woven twig pad, a curved scrap of mottled shell, a tuft of brown-and-white hair.
docs.body:
FOUND WHERE THE TRAIL MEETS THE RIVER
[[c:twigs|1. Twigs of myrtle and tamarisk, woven tight like a basket.]]
[[c:shell|2. A scrap of old tortoise shell. Small holes are bored along one edge.]]
3. Cow hairs, brown and white. Apollo's, surely.
[[c:river|Here the cow prints go on along the river.]]
[[c:split|The brushy prints turn off alone, up towards Mount Cyllene.]]
— Kleon

docs.title: Notice
docs.author: the hall of Zeus
docs.where: it floats down on a small white cloud and hovers at the child's eye level until read
docs.picture: a scroll tied with a gold thread, resting on a cloud the size of a pillow.
docs.body:
FROM THE HALL OF ZEUS, ON OLYMPUS
[[c:judge-sunset|Zeus will hear the matter of Apollo's cattle at sunset.]]
[[c:summons-om|The old man of Onchestus must come and say what he saw.]]
[[c:vines-ate|Apollo says his cows ate the old man's vines last spring.]]
[[c:pay|If no thief is named, the old man's vineyard goes to Apollo.]]
It will pay for the lost herd.
A cloud will carry all who are called.

docs.title: Tablet
docs.author: Maia
docs.where: hung on a peg at the mouth of a cave high on Mount Cyllene
docs.picture: a small, worn wax tablet hanging by a cord, a sprig of wild olive tied to it, the cave mouth dark behind.
docs.body:
Hush. A baby sleeps here.
[[c:born-dawn|My son was born at dawn yesterday.]]
[[c:not-stirred|He has not stirred from his cradle since.]]
Please knock softly.
Better still, do not knock at all.
— Maia, of the cave on Mount Cyllene

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: What did you see last night?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
I saw vines. A great many vines.
My eyes are old, and the moon was thin.
[[c:om-staff|Someone went by with a staff, walking from side to side.]]
That is all. That is quite enough.

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: Who was it?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
Who? I could not say.
[[c:om-promise|I made a promise last night, and I keep my promises. Mostly.]]
Do not ask me what I promised. That is part of the promise.

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: What were you doing out so late?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
[[c:om-brush|Cutting brushwood, to tie up my vines.]]
I had bundles of it, all evening long.
Brushwood gets everywhere. In my beard, in my hat, in my supper.

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: Do you like Apollo's cows?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
Like them? [[c:om-vines|They ate my best vines last spring!]]
Every leaf. Every grape. I wept like a fountain.
But a cow? I wouldn't know where to keep one. Fifty would be a whole town.

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: What sandals do you wear?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
[[c:om-feet|Plain leather ones. And my feet are as big as loaves.]]
I have walked these rows for seventy years.
Leather lasts. So do I.

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: When did the someone pass?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
[[c:om-moonrise|After moonrise. Long after sunset.]]
I was tying the last row.
[[c:om-hum|The someone hummed a little tune, very pleased with the night.]]

docs.title: Maia: Where is your son?
docs.author: Maia
docs.body:
In his cradle, the little lamb, fast asleep.
[[c:maia-dawn|At dawn today I looked in, and there he was, wrapped up tight.]]

docs.title: Maia: When did you see him before that?
docs.author: Maia
docs.body:
Before that?
[[c:maia-yday|Yesterday at dawn, when I laid him down.]]
Then I had things to do.
[[c:maia-dodge|A baby one day old? Where would he go?]]

docs.title: Maia: What things did you have to do?
docs.author: Maia
docs.body:
Things. A mother has things.
[[c:maia-things|I was not in the cave all day. That is all I will say.]]

docs.title: Maia: Why do you live up here?
docs.author: Maia
docs.body:
It is quiet, and it is ours.
[[c:maia-cave|But it is cold, and we have no herds, no gold, no honours.]]
My son's big brother has all three.

docs.title: Maia: What was that sound?
docs.author: Maia
docs.body:
What sound? I hear nothing.
*(From the cradle: plink.)*
[[c:maia-wind|That is the wind. The wind on this mountain is very musical.]]

docs.title: Hermes: Where were you last night?
docs.author: Hermes
docs.body:
Here! In my cradle! Where else does a baby go?
I am very small. Look at me. Tiny.

docs.title: Hermes: Do you know anything about fifty cows?
docs.author: Hermes
docs.body:
Cows? What are cows? Are they nice?
[[c:her-born|I was born yesterday! My feet are soft, and the ground is rough.]]
I care about milk, and sleep, and warm blankets.

docs.title: Hermes: Do you know the old man with the vines?
docs.author: Hermes
docs.body:
Never met him!
[[c:her-onchestus|I have never even been to Onchestus.]]
*(Nell, slowly: "Nobody said Onchestus.")*

docs.title: Hermes: What's under your blanket?
docs.author: Hermes
docs.body:
Nothing. *(twang)* A hiccup. Babies hiccup.
[[c:her-twang|Musical hiccups. I was born with them.]]

docs.title: Hermes: What do you want, little one?
docs.author: Hermes
docs.body:
[[c:her-want|A herd of my own one day. And honour, like my big brother.]]
Not cows, of course. Something like cows. Honour.

docs.title: Hermes: The persona question
docs.author: Hermes
docs.body:
Nobody! I mean, nothing! I saw nothing.
[[c:her-saw|I saw nothing, just like the old man.]]
*(He claps both hands over his mouth. Plink.)*

docs.title: Apollo: Could a wolf have taken them?
docs.author: Apollo
docs.body:
A wolf takes one calf and runs. Fifty cows?
[[c:apollo-never|And I have never seen prints like those. Not in all my days.]]
They make my hair stand up. Look. Up.

docs.title: The old man of Onchestus: Please. Who went by your vines?
docs.author: The old man of Onchestus
docs.body:
Oh, very well. A promise to a cow-thief is a thin sort of promise.
[[c:om-knee|He was no taller than my knee.]]
[[c:om-heads|He walked the cows tail first, with their heads towards him.]]
[[c:om-told|He said, "You saw nothing, grandfather." So I tried to see nothing.]]
It is very hard, seeing nothing. My eyes kept seeing things.

docs.title: Maia: Maia, where were you yesterday?
docs.author: Maia
docs.body:
On the mountaintop, with my six sisters.
[[c:maia-sisters|I left him asleep and sat with them until the stars came out.]]
I was ashamed to say so. What mother leaves a baby one day old?
[[c:maia-believed|I believed he slept. I did not see him sleep.]]

deductions.label: the impossible thing
deductions.statement: Every hoof-print points into the meadow, but the meadow is empty. Fifty cows cannot walk in and vanish. So they were walked out backwards, tails first. Someone wanted the tracks to lie.
deductions.why: tracks are a text. Read on their own, these say "fifty cows walked in". Read with the empty meadow, they say the opposite. Two true sentences that cannot both be the whole truth mean somebody was clever.

deductions.label: the disguise
deductions.statement: The odd prints are not a strange creature's. They are twig pads, woven like a basket and tied over a very small foot. Whoever drove the cows hid his own steps, and his foot was tiny.
deductions.why: this is Nell's false link turned round. Brushwood is in the prints, but a basket of twigs is something worn, not something carried. And the dent inside is no bigger than a fig. The old man's feet are "as big as loaves".

deductions.label: the alibi
deductions.statement: Maia says her son has not stirred since dawn yesterday. But yesterday at noon a new sound came from the south, a sound like a singing bowstring. A scrap of shell with string-holes lies by the river. And the cradle twangs. Someone in that cave was very busy yesterday.
deductions.why: "He has not stirred" is what Maia believes, and she only looked twice: at dawn yesterday and at dawn today. Between those two looks lies a whole day she cannot speak for. The noon sound fills it.

wrongLinks.quill: Brushwood in a bundle, or brushwood on a foot? Read the finds list.

events.text: The baby is born in the cave; Maia lays him down and goes to her sisters
A new sound, like a singing bowstring, comes from the south
Apollo counts fifty cows in the meadow
Apollo goes up to Olympus to sing
The cows are walked out of the empty meadow, tails first
events.timeWords: (no time word: the gap between 4 and 6)

events.text: Someone knee-high passes the vines at Onchestus, humming
The cows go on along the river; the brushy prints turn up the mountain
Maia looks in: the baby is wrapped up tight
Apollo comes back to an empty meadow

shake.quill: Can anyone make music before they are born? Even here?

wrongSuspect.oldman: How tall was the someone? Read what he said on the cloud. Then look at the dent in the middle of each print.
wrongSuspect.maia: Where was Maia all day? Up a mountain, with six witnesses who happen to be stars. And what did she actually see?

wolf.quill: No wolf walks cattle backwards, and none left a print. Read Kleon's first tablet.
wolf.name: the wolf

lost-count.quill: He counted fifty yesterday afternoon. He wrote it down. Find me fifty cows.
lost-count.name: Apollo lost count

accusation.weakEvidence: You've shown the cows went out backwards. Now: whose foot fits inside a basket of twigs, with a dent no bigger than a fig? And who was awake at noon?
accusation.note: Hermes, one day old, who made the first lyre by noon, walked Apollo's fifty cows out of the meadow backwards that evening, wearing woven twig pads over his small feet, hid them by the river, and was back in his cradle before morning.

reveal.text: Little detective from the other side of the page. Who took the cattle?
Hermes.

reveal.direction: Silence. Then the cradle says: plink.

reveal.text: A baby? He was born yesterday!
I was! Exactly! Thank you!
First, the tracks. Every hoof-print points into the meadow, and the meadow is empty. Fifty cows can't walk in and vanish. So they were walked out backwards, tails first.
And the odd prints are twig pads. Woven like a basket, tied over a foot no bigger than a fig. The old man's feet are as big as loaves.
Bigger, on a hot day.
The old man had a secret, but it wasn't a crime. He promised to see nothing, and he kept trying.
Very hard work.
Maia had a secret too. She spent the day with her sisters, and she believed her son slept. She never saw it.
And at dawn today I heard the latch. I told myself it was the wind.
And the last clue was there from the very first page. Apollo wrote: "Yesterday at noon I heard a new sound from the south." A bowstring that had learned to sing.

reveal.direction: Kleon holds up the first tablet. The noon line glows. Then the cradle twangs, and the two moments sit side by side.

reveal.text: Oh, all right.

reveal.direction: He holds up a tortoise shell with two curved arms and seven strings: the first lyre.

reveal.text: I found an old shell by the cave at dawn. By noon it could sing. By evening I was bored. You have temples and gold, big brother. I have a cold cave. I wanted a herd, and honour.

reveal.direction: Zeus begins to rumble. The rumble becomes a laugh. Zeus laughs so hard the clouds wobble.

reveal.text: Born yesterday! Show your brother where the cows are, little one.

reveal.direction: A page turns. A high cave by a river. Fifty cows, all fine, chewing, faintly offended at being found.

reveal.text: Fifty! …fifty.

reveal.direction: Hermes plucks the lyre. A slow, bright tune fills the cave. Apollo sits down on a rock without meaning to.

reveal.text: What is that? I have never heard anything like it.
A trade? The lyre for the herd.
Done. And no more tricks.
Fewer tricks.
Fewer. Correct.

reveal.direction: Apollo plays. The cows stop chewing to listen. The old man of Onchestus puts his hat back on and goes home to his vines, which Apollo has promised to leave alone.

epilogue.text: The friendship. Back on the hillside, the two brothers walk ahead, Apollo playing badly and then less badly, Hermes correcting him. Kleon writes a new tablet: "Apollo's cattle: found. Apollo: musical." In the Greek myths, Apollo becomes the god of music, and Hermes the messenger of the gods and the keeper of herds.
The souvenir. As the sun touches the hills, Hermes holds something out to {det}: a small, smooth pick cut from the same old shell.
For plucking. It's called a… I haven't named it yet. You name it.
We've got a word. Felix will tell you. At length. The Door's light flickers. Sunset. Nell grabs {det}'s sleeve, and they step through.

The new shelf. In the office, a narrow shelf has appeared beside the Door, where yesterday there was only wall. The tortoise-shell plectrum goes on it, first of four empty places. When you tap it, it plays one bright note.
Footnote: plectrum, from Greek plēktron, "a thing to strike with". Footnote to the footnote: it means you strike the string, not the tortoise.
Bring back what you learned, not what you found. One exception. Just this once.
Nell's thread. Nell sits on the office floor with her back to the Door.
I said ten. About an old man who was keeping a promise.
And then I didn't say a number. Not yet.
epilogue.direction: She takes the Inspector form out of her basket, looks at it, and puts it back.

epilogue.text: Biscuit. Constable Tully puffs up all 39 stairs. "He's gone again." Biscuit is found asleep on the new shelf, curled round the plectrum, smelling faintly of wild thyme. Nobody can work out how he got through a door that was shut.
The calling card. Dev comes up last, with a bun. He stops in the doorway.

Was this here when you left? On the floorboards, just inside the office door, lies a small waxed card with a perfect ink blot. It was not there a moment ago. The stairs are empty. The air smells faintly of rosin, like a violin case just opened.
Every track points somewhere. Follow it forthwith. — B.
It's not a word. There's no gap anywhere.
It's not for the Ledger. It's for us.
epilogue.direction: He turns it over.; Nobody says anything. Down on the quay, very faint, someone is tuning a violin.

drill.title: Which Way Did They Go?
drill.intro: Track Reader. Five short track descriptions slide onto the desk. For each, the child drags a little cow token the way the animal really went, then taps the words that prove it.

items.prompt: Hoof-prints point into the barn. The barn is empty.
Paw-prints go into the shed and come back out.
Boot prints lead to the pond. A wet boot is on the bank.
items.answer: to the pond, then off without one boot
items.proof: "A wet boot is on the bank."

items.prompt: Bird prints stop in the middle of the snow.
Hoof-prints point north. Every one is pressed deepest at the front.
items.answer: north, the ordinary way (a fair check, so the child doesn't answer "backwards" every time)

marginNotes.text: The Hymn to Hermes is one of the "Homeric Hymns", a set of old Greek poems once credited to Homer, though scholars agree he did not write them. It tells Hermes's first day in one line: "Born with the dawning, at mid-day he played on the lyre, and in the evening he stole the cattle of far-shooting Apollo."
marginNotes.source: Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes, lines 17–18, trans. H. G. Evelyn-White (Loeb Classical Library, 1914). (This note opens only after Case Closed, because it names the thief. Before then the tab reads: "The poem this Journey comes from is about 2,500 years old. Its name is a spoiler. Solve it first.")

marginNotes.text: People say "I wasn't born yesterday!" to mean "you can't fool me". In the hymn, baby Hermes says the opposite, and means it literally: he really was born the day before. The English saying is much younger than the poem, a happy coincidence and not its origin.
marginNotes.source: Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes, about line 273, trans. Evelyn-White (1914): "I was born yesterday, and my feet are soft and the ground beneath is rough"; for the idiom, the Oxford English Dictionary, "yesterday" and "born" (writer to check the first recorded date before ship). [VERIFY: the idiom's first recorded date, and that it is not derived from the hymn.]

marginNotes.text: The oldest Greek lyres were made with a tortoise shell for the sound-box. Greek even had a word for that kind of lyre: chelys, which also means "tortoise". From lyre English gets lyric, the words of a song.
marginNotes.source: M. L. West, Ancient Greek Music (Oxford, 1992), ch. 3, on the chelys-lyre; Oxford English Dictionary and Merriam-Webster, "lyric".

marginNotes.text: In the hymn, the cattle travel from Pieria, near Mount Olympus, all the way to the river Alpheus in the south, past Onchestus, in a single night: hundreds of miles. Only a poem can move fifty cows that fast, and the hymn enjoys saying so.
marginNotes.source: Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes, lines 68–104 (the night drive), trans. Evelyn-White (1914); Pieria, Onchestus, Cyllene and the Alpheus on any atlas of ancient Greece, e.g. R. J. A. Talbert (ed.), Barrington Atlas of the Greek and Roman World (Princeton, 2000).

marginNotes.text: (chapter 5 margin note, after Case Closed) In the hymn, when Hermes plays the lyre, Apollo is so delighted that he says the music is worth fifty cows, and the trade is made. Apollo also gives his little brother a shining staff, and Hermes becomes the herdsman of the gods. Two brothers who began with a theft end as lifelong friends.
marginNotes.source: Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes, lines 436–580 (the lyre, the trade and the gifts), trans. Evelyn-White (1914).

line.text: What's not on this page? Not one print points out.
So what it actually says is: 'I'm too little to have walked anywhere.' That's a big thing for a small person to say.
We've seen that word before. Noon.
Something happened here, between sunset and moonrise, and nobody's told us.
If I were Maia, what would I have seen? A sleeping baby. Twice.
Listen to how he says it. 'The ground is rough.' Only someone who has stood on it says that.

path: Greek plēktron, "a thing to strike with" (from plēssein, "to strike")
bonusCard.story: A plectrum is the small pick a player uses to pluck a lyre, a harp or a guitar. The Greek word means "a thing to strike with", because you strike the string.

exercises.prompt: "Kleon is Apollo's herald. He reads the news out loud." A herald is…
exercises.explain: The next sentence tells you. Kleon reads the news out loud. A herald brings news and says it for everyone to hear.

exercises.prompt: Put Apollo's day in order, first to last.
options: He went to Olympus at sunset.
He found the meadow empty at dawn.
answer: He went to Olympus at sunset.
He found the meadow empty at dawn.
exercises.explain: The tablet says "yesterday afternoon", then "at sunset", then "at dawn". Afternoon comes before sunset. Dawn is the next morning.

exercises.prompt: "Like a broom that walked." Did a broom really walk?
options: No, the prints only looked brushy
No, a cow swept the path
exercises.answer: No, the prints only looked brushy
exercises.explain: "Like" tells you it is a picture in words. The prints were brushy at the edges, as if a broom had feet.

exercises.prompt: Maia writes: "Please knock softly. Better still, do not knock." What does she want?
exercises.explain: Her first line is "Hush. A baby sleeps here." She would rather nobody knocked at all.

exercises.prompt: The old man says: "I made a promise, and I keep my promises. Mostly." What did he NOT say?
options: who he made the promise to
exercises.answer: who he made the promise to
exercises.explain: He tells you there was a promise, and when. He does not say who it was for. What a person leaves out can be a clue.

exercises.prompt: "They ate my best vines! I wept like a fountain." What does "wept like a fountain" mean?
exercises.explain: A fountain pours out water. Weeping like one means a great many tears. It is a simile, a picture made with "like".

exercises.prompt: Which came first: the new sound at noon, or Apollo going to Olympus?
options: they happened at the same time
exercises.explain: Noon is the middle of the day. Apollo left at sunset, at the end of the day. Time-words like "noon" and "sunset" let you order events.

exercises.prompt: "A scrap of old tortoise shell. Small holes are bored along one edge." Here, "bored" means…
options: made with a tool that turns
exercises.answer: made with a tool that turns
exercises.explain: A hole can be bored with a drill. "Bored" can also mean fed up, but a shell cannot be fed up. The words around a word tell you which meaning fits.

exercises.prompt: In the Greek myths, the Muses were goddesses of the arts. Which English word comes from their name?
exercises.explain: Greek mousikē meant "the art of the Muses". Museum comes from the same family: a home of the Muses.

exercises.prompt: Put these four sentences in order to retell the hymn's first day.
options: That evening, Apollo's cattle were walked away backwards.
At noon, a new sound came from a cave in the south.
Before morning, the cradle was full again.
At dawn, a baby was born on Mount Cyllene.
answer: At dawn, a baby was born on Mount Cyllene.
At noon, a new sound came from a cave in the south.
That evening, Apollo's cattle were walked away backwards.
Before morning, the cradle was full again.
exercises.explain: The time-words carry the order: at dawn, at noon, that evening, before morning. A good summary keeps only the big steps.

exercises.prompt: Nobody had told the baby where the old man lives. Yet he said, "I have never even been to Onchestus." Why does that matter?
options: He knew a place he should not have known
exercises.answer: He knew a place he should not have known
exercises.explain: A person can give themselves away by knowing too much. Nobody had said "Onchestus" to him. So how did he know?

exercises.prompt: Lyre is the Greek harp that Hermes made. Which word for the words of a song comes from it?
exercises.explain: Songs were once sung to the lyre, so their words were "lyric" words. Lyrebird is named after the instrument too, but it is a bird, not the words of a song. Liar is a different family altogether.
